chapters.title: Chapter 6: Cash Flow Management in Practice

lessons.title: How Every Department Affects Cash: Sales, Procurement, HR and Operations

children.text: Ask most Indian companies who manages cash and the answer is the finance team. That answer is wrong in a specific and expensive way. Finance measures cash, reports it and arranges funding for the gap. The decisions that create the gap are made by a sales head agreeing terms, a procurement manager taking a discount, an HR team confirming joining dates and a plant head deciding what to build. By the time finance sees the number, every one of those decisions is already made.

body.text: Nobody in finance can collect an invoice on terms sales agreed, unbuy stock procurement ordered, or unhire people HR onboarded. Cash is decided upstream and merely reported downstream.

children.text: The Same Company, Four Departments, One Bank Account
Every example below has appeared earlier in this course. Put them side by side and the pattern is unmistakable.

body.caption: Ordinary decisions and what they cost in cash

cells: Give the largest dealer 90-day terms instead of 60
Buy three months of glaze instead of one, for an 8% discount
₹43.3 lakh locked, ₹9.3 lakh a year to carry
Onboard 25 engineers before the client contract bills
About ₹1 crore of payroll funded before the first receipt
Build festive stock ahead of confirmed orders
₹12 lakh of inventory in one month
Pay micro and small suppliers within 45 days
₹18.9 lakh of cash used, and compliance achieved

stats.label: Decided inside finance
stats.context: The one row finance actually controls

stats.label: Who gets asked about cash
stats.context: Usually after the money has gone

body.text: None of those four decisions was wrong. Longer terms win dealers, bulk buying is cheaper, engineers have to be hired before a project delivers, and festive stock must exist before Diwali. The failure is not the decisions, it is that each was made without anyone stating its cash price out loud.

children.text: Why Good People Make Cash-Destroying Decisions
Look at what each function is measured on, and the behaviour stops being mysterious.

body.caption: The measurement, and the behaviour it produces

cells: Terms are conceded to close deals, and March billing spikes with cash arriving in June
Bulk orders and early payment discounts, both of which consume cash
Long runs and healthy buffers, which become inventory
Time to fill roles and offer acceptance
Joining dates cluster ahead of revenue, and payroll rises before billing does
Safety stock on everything, including slow items

body.text: The sharpest example is the sales incentive. If commission is paid on invoices raised, the company is literally paying people to create receivables. If it is paid on cash collected, the same people become the most effective collections team in the business, because they have relationships nobody in accounts has.

body.title: Two versions of the same incentive scheme

columns.label: Commission on billing
points: Paid when the invoice is raised
Credit terms become a negotiating giveaway
Collections are seen as the accounts team's problem
Bad debts are discovered long after commission is paid

columns.label: Commission on collection
points: Terms are negotiated carefully, because they delay payout
The relationship owner makes the collection call
Doubtful customers are screened before supply, not after

body.title: What would a collections culture be worth?
body.prompt: Konkan Ceramics has ₹12 crore of annual sales and days sales outstanding of 73. If a collection-linked incentive brings that down to 60 days, how much cash does it release, in ₹ lakh? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: One day of sales is ₹12 crore divided by 365, about ₹3.29 lakh. Thirteen days released is about ₹42.7 lakh, which appears in the bank once and stays there as long as the discipline holds. That is roughly a third of the company's annual profit, produced by changing when a commission is paid rather than by selling anything more.

body.title: Where cash is decided
body.textWithBlank: Finance reports and funds the cash gap, but the gap itself is created ___ of finance, by the decisions of sales, procurement, production and HR.
body.explanation: This is why cash discipline cannot be delegated to the finance team. Every function needs one cash metric it owns, expressed in its own language and reviewed alongside its other targets.

children.text: Cash improves when each function has a metric it owns, understands and is reviewed on. One metric each, not a dashboard.

cells: Days sales outstanding and the value overdue beyond 60 days, by territory
Inventory days for the categories they buy, and terms achieved against target
Slow-moving and dead stock as a share of total inventory
Payroll and statutory outflow forecast accuracy, and joining dates matched to billing
Capex payment dates forecast against actual
Forecast accuracy, statutory payments made on time, and cost of funds

body.title: Making the metric land with people who do not like finance

children.text: Three translation habits do most of the work.
Convert days into rupees, every time.
"Reduce DSO by 13 days" means nothing to a sales manager. "₹42.7 lakh, which is about a third of our annual profit" means something.
Give the east region head the east region ageing report, not the company total. Ownership needs a number the person can actually move.

When a dealer asks for 30 extra days, the conversation changes once the ₹16.4 lakh and the ₹1.8 lakh of annual interest are on the table. Most people will not concede terms casually once the price is visible.

One caution. Metrics create behaviour, including behaviour you did not intend. A hard DSO target can push a sales team into refusing legitimate credit and losing good customers, and a hard inventory target can create stock-outs. Pair every cash metric with the business metric it could damage, and review both together.

body.title: A monthly cash rhythm that actually works

events.title: Cash meeting, 30 minutes
events.description: Finance presents the updated 13-week forecast. Sales calls over the top 20 collections by name. Anything that moved by more than an agreed threshold is explained.

events.title: Statutory block
events.description: Payroll, then TDS by the 7th. These are funded first, before any discretionary payment is released.

events.title: Ageing review
events.description: Receivables ageing circulated to each territory head, and payables ageing checked against MSME timelines.

events.title: Purchase and capex commitments
events.description: Procurement and projects confirm what will be committed, with expected payment dates, before orders are placed.

events.title: Forecast against actual
events.description: Last month's forecast compared with what happened, line by line, and the learning fed into next month's numbers.

body.text: Thirty minutes a week is the entire time commitment, and the agenda is fixed: what did we forecast, what actually happened, what changed, and what are we doing about the trough. Companies that hold this meeting consistently rarely have cash surprises, because a surprise requires nobody to have been looking.

body.title: Find the root cause
body.question: Receivables have grown for three straight quarters while sales are flat. The collections team has been strengthened twice and nothing has improved. What is the most likely root cause to investigate?
options: The collections team needs better software
Customers in this industry simply pay slowly
Sales incentives are paid on billing, and credit terms are being conceded without approval
The finance team is not escalating overdue accounts quickly enough
body.explanation: When strengthening collections twice changes nothing, the problem is upstream of collections. Receivables grow because of what was agreed at the point of sale: terms conceded to close deals, credit extended to customers who should not have it, and no consequence for either. Software and escalation improve execution. They cannot fix an incentive that rewards creating receivables.

body.title: HR is asked to make the workforce cash-aware
body.scenario: You lead HR and learning at a 400-person manufacturing company. The CFO says cash discipline is weak across the business and asks you to "run some training on cash flow". The managing director wants something measurable within two quarters, not a workshop that everyone enjoys and nobody applies.
body.prompt: What would you actually design, beyond a training session?
body.modelAnswer:
Accept the brief, then widen it, because training alone will not move a number.
1. Diagnose first. Ask finance for the three cash metrics that have deteriorated most, and the rupee value of each. Training built on the company's own numbers lands differently from generic content.
2. Segment the audience. Sales managers, procurement, plant and stores heads, and finance each need a different 90 minutes. A single company-wide session teaches everyone things that are not their job.
3. Teach in their currency. For sales, the ageing report and what 13 days is worth. For procurement, carrying cost against discount, and the MSME timeline. For stores, dead stock. Use live company data, anonymised if needed.
Then change the system, which is the part that actually works.
4. Work with finance and the CFO on the incentive question: commission on collection rather than billing, even partially, and a credit approval step that sits outside the sales line.
5. Add one cash metric to each function head's scorecard, agreed with them, with a business metric paired against it so nobody optimises cash at the cost of the business.
6. Fix what HR itself owns: give finance a rolling payroll and statutory forecast, align joining dates with billing milestones, and flag bonus and full and final settlement timing well in advance.
7. Put HR into the weekly cash meeting. If HR is absent, payroll timing is an assumption rather than a commitment.
Then make it measurable.
8. Baseline the three metrics now and report them monthly for two quarters. Success is DSO down, dead stock down and forecast accuracy up, not attendance or feedback scores.
9. Run a short refresher at the one-quarter mark using the actual movement in those numbers, so people see the consequence of their own behaviour.
10. Be honest with the CFO about the causality. If incentives do not change, training will produce awareness and very little else, and that should be said before the programme starts, not after it is judged.

body.title: Set up the weekly cash meeting
steps: Fix a standing 30-minute slot on the same day each week, with the same attendees from finance, sales, procurement, production and HR.
Circulate the updated 13-week forecast before the meeting, not during it.
Open with last week's forecast against actual, and name what moved and why.
Call over the top 20 collections by customer name, with the relationship owner answering, not the accounts team.
Review upcoming commitments: purchase orders, capex milestones, hiring, so they enter the forecast before they are made.
Confirm statutory dates for the coming fortnight and that they are funded.
End on one number: the forecast trough, the week it falls in and the headroom against sanctioned limits.
Record decisions and owners in five lines, and start the next meeting with them.

body.title: Cash as a Team Sport: Key Terms

cards.definition: A commercial or operational choice that commits cash long before finance sees it.
Paying sales incentives when money arrives rather than when an invoice is raised.
Deciding customer credit limits outside the sales reporting line, so terms are not a negotiating giveaway.
One cash number per function, expressed in their language and reviewed with their other targets.
The business measure reviewed alongside a cash metric, so nobody optimises cash at the cost of sales or service.
A fixed 30-minute review of forecast against actual, collections, commitments and the trough.

points: Finance reports and funds the cash gap. Sales, procurement, production and HR create it, and they create it first.
In the examples from this course, about ₹1.72 crore of cash was committed by decisions taken outside finance, against ₹18.9 lakh inside it.
People behave as they are measured. Commission on billing pays a team to manufacture receivables.
Switching to collection-linked incentives and cutting DSO from 73 to 60 days releases about ₹42.7 lakh at Konkan Ceramics.
Give each function one cash metric it owns, paired with the business metric it could damage.
Thirty minutes every Monday, with a fixed agenda and the right people in the room, prevents most cash surprises.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional and all figures are illustrative, carried forward from earlier lessons for continuity. Incentive structures should be designed with your HR, finance and legal teams and must comply with applicable employment terms.
